nameStory: The name 'groundhog' comes from this chunky rodent's habit of living in underground burrows and its pig-like grunting sounds when alarmed. It's also called 'woodchuck,' which comes from the Algonquian word 'wuchak,' though despite the famous tongue-twister, woodchucks don't actually chuck wood!
description: The groundhog is a stocky, barrel-shaped rodent about the size of a small dog, weighing 4-14 pounds. This largest member of the squirrel family has coarse, grizzled brown fur that looks frosted with lighter tips, short legs, and a moderately bushy tail. Unlike their mountain-dwelling marmot cousins, groundhogs prefer lowland areas and are surprisingly solitary for such social-looking animals. You'll often spot them sitting upright like sentries near their burrow entrances.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Compact and chunky with a low-slung body, about the size of a small dog but much rounder. Short, powerful legs make them appear to waddle when walking.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Coarse, grizzled brown coat with individual hairs banded in dark and light colors, giving a 'salt and pepper' frosted appearance. The fur feels rough and bristly if you ever handle one.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen sitting bolt upright on hind legs like a prairie dog, scanning for danger. When alarmed, they emit a sharp whistle before diving into their burrows.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Four toes on front feet, five on back, with long claws for digging. Front prints about 2 inches long, showing prominent claw marks in soft soil.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Large burrow entrances 10-12 inches wide with excavated soil piles nearby. Scat is dark, oval pellets often found near burrow openings.

habitat: Groundhogs prefer open woodlands, field edges, and grassy areas near forest borders throughout New England's lowlands. They especially love spots where they can dig burrows in well-drained soil on gentle slopes, with nearby access to both cover and open feeding areas. You'll often find them in agricultural areas, suburban parks, and along woodland clearings.

seasonality.spring: Emerging from hibernation in March-April, groundhogs are most active and visible as they rebuild energy reserves. This is when you're most likely to see them out in the open during midday.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with frequent above-ground foraging, especially in early morning and late afternoon. Young groundhogs disperse from maternal burrows, making family groups more visible.
seasonality.fall: Feeding heavily to build fat reserves for winter hibernation, often becoming quite bold about foraging in open areas. Their fur appears thickest and most grizzled during this season.
seasonality.winter: True hibernators, groundhogs are rarely seen from November through February. Any winter sightings are unusual and worth noting, as it may indicate a disturbed burrow.

funFact: Groundhogs are true hibernators whose body temperature drops to just above freezing, their heart rate slows from 80 beats per minute to just 5, and they can lose up to half their body weight during their 5-month winter sleep!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with beavers when seen on land, but groundhogs have much smaller, less paddle-like tails and are never found far from their terrestrial burrows. Remember: if it's waddling through your garden, it's probably a groundhog; if it's near water with a flat tail, it's a beaver.
contextualKnowledge: Despite Punxsutawney Phil's fame, groundhogs don't actually predict weather—they emerge based on soil temperature and internal biological clocks, not shadow-seeing abilities. The whole Groundhog Day tradition is a fun cultural twist on the natural timing of their hibernation cycle.
compareHints: Groundhogs are the only marmots in New England, making them unique among their genus here. Compared to other large squirrel family members like woodchucks or tree squirrels, groundhogs are much more terrestrial and stockier, lacking the agility and tree-climbing abilities of their cousins. Their closest behavioral relatives in the region would be beavers, but groundhogs are strictly land-dwelling burrow engineers rather than aquatic dam builders.
